Abstract
Flexible circuits that allow stable electrical conductance and signal transmission under deformation are highly
required for flexible electronics. However, bending-induced fatigue cracks in solid conductive materials can
significantly reduce the stability of flexible circuits. Although liquid metal (LM) is a promising candidate for
bending-resistant circuits, LM circuits are prone to being squeezed and susceptible to compression. Here, an
extremely bending-resistant and compression-insensitive flexible circuit was achieved by the complementary
effects of the fluidity of the upper LM and the good conductivity and rigidity of a thick bottom copper (Cu)
layer. The fluidic LM can heal Cu cracks in real-time by spontaneous interfacial wetting to enhance the
bending durability, whereas the solid Cu layer can maintain conductivity under compression to enhance the
compression insensitivity. Compared with a conventional Cu circuit, such a flexible circuit achieves a
120-fold improvement in folding lifespan, while its resistance fluctuation under compression is only 0.05% of
that of the counterpart LM circuit. Meanwhile, the bottom Cu pattern exactly facilitates the high-resolution
selective printing of LM by reactive wetting. As a demonstration, a flexible signal acquisition system
constructed with this circuit can continuously capture pulse signals during bending and remain functional after
10 000 bending cycles. The simultaneously enhanced bending stability and compression insensitivity greatly
increase the applicability and reliability of flexible circuits under various deformation conditions.

1. Introduction
Flexible circuits are widely used in foldable optoelectronic displays [1-5], stretchable electronics [6-8],
flexible sensors [9-12], and wearable medical diagnostic systems [13-15], serving for reliable electrical
interconnection and stable electrical signal transmission. Owing to their high conductivity, mechanical
deformability, and compatibility with high-resolution and high-throughput established manufacturing
processes, laminated rigid metal thin films (copper (Cu), gold (Au), aluminum (Al), etc.) with polymer
substrates (polyimide (PI), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), etc.) have long been mainstream
configurations in current practical flexible circuits [16-19]. However, the inherent requirement for
deformability of flexible electronics poses a challenge to the stability and durability of such flexible circuits,
as repeated mechanical stress is prone to induce cracks within the metal films [20, 21]. Such undesirable
mechanical failures can lead to resistance drift, fluctuations, or even complete loss in electrical conductivity,
severely affecting the functions and lifespan of flexible electronics. To suppress crack propagation, great
efforts have been made by inserting another interlayer [22-24] or enhancing interface adhesion [25-30],
which can effectively reduce the practical strain on the metal film or prevent local stress concentration,
enabling the flexible circuits to withstand greater applied strain without cracking. Even so, it is worth noting
that repeated small strain cycles, even below the fracture strain of metal film, can also induce fatigue cracks
during long-term stress cycles due to the mechanical mismatch between the stiff metal film and the
compliant substrate [20, 31]. Therefore, an effective strategy to improve long-term fatigue durability and
prolong the lifespan of flexible circuits is urgently needed.
In recent years, due to its high fluidity and self-healing capability, liquid metal (LM) has emerged as a
promising candidate for enhancing the durability of flexible circuits [32]. A common configuration is
LM-elastomer composite featured LM microcapsules embedded in the elastomer matrix, which can release
LM and bridge the conductive pathways to restore electrical functionality when the LM microcapsules are
damaged [33-36]. However, patterning such materials into conductive flexible circuits still faces limitations
in resolution and efficiency, such as the limited resolution of stencil printing, complex matching of multiple
process parameters (nozzle diameter, nozzle height, flow speed, etc.), and inherent efficiency constraints of
serial inkjet printing [37-41]. In recent years, laser scribing has also been employed as an effective method
for circuit patterning due to its mask‑free advantage [42-45]. However, this process may face issues such as
droplet spreading or the risk of ablating the substrate. Reactive wetting with metal films offers an efficient
method for printing high-resolution pure LM circuits [46-50]. By inheriting the inherent high precision of
the photolithography process [51, 52], this method can be used to fabricate very fine LM circuits based on
high-precision metal patterns prepared by photolithography. Such LM circuits offer excellent stretching and
bending performances, but an often neglected issue is their susceptibility to compression. The conductivity
of such circuits is provided mainly by the thicker LM layer, as the metal film is often very thin (at the

Here, we propose an extremely bending-resistant and compression-insensitive flexible circuit by the
complementary effects of the fluidity of the upper LM and the good conductivity and rigidity of a thick bottom
copper (Cu) layer. The highly fluidic LM can timely heal the cracks in the Cu layer during bending by
spontaneous interfacial wetting to enhance the bending durability, whereas the highly conductive thick Cu
layer can maintain conductivity under compression to enhance the compression insensitivity. Compared with
the counterpart Cu circuits, the obtained flexible circuits exhibit a durability of 230 000 cycles under a
bending radius of 0.5 mm and 60 000 cycles under repeated folding conditions, achieving an improvement of
2.3 and 120 times, respectively. Moreover, its resistance fluctuation under compression (4 MPa) is only 0.05%
that of the counterpart LM circuit. Meanwhile, the bottom Cu pattern exactly facilitates the high-resolution
and high-efficiency selective printing of LM by reactive wetting. As a proof of concept, such a robust flexible
circuit was integrated into a flexible system for acquiring human pulse signals, which can continuously collect
pulse signals during bending with negligible interference and operate normally even after 10 000 bending
cycles. The excellent bending durability and compression insensitivity greatly enhance the applicability and
reliability of flexible circuits under various deformation conditions.
2. Results and discussion
Figure 1(a) illustrates the structure and advantage of the bending-resistant and compression-insensitive
flexible circuit enabled by real-time crack healing of the bottom Cu layer by spontaneous interfacial wetting of
the upper LM. For conventional flexible circuits consisting of rigid metal films and polymer substrates, cracks
often propagate in the metal films during repeated bending cycles due to interface delamination, excessive
local stress, or fatigue damage (Figure 1(a-i)), leading to abrupt resistance change or even complete loss of
electrical functionality, which severely affects the continuous operation stability and lifespan of the electronic
systems. As a potential alternative to solid metal circuits, LM circuits exhibit good bending stability owing to
their excellent fluidity. However, this also causes the LM channels to be prone to undergoing a significant
reduction in cross-sectional area under compression, making the resistance of the circuit highly susceptible to
pressure (Figure 1(a-ii)). To address this conflict, we propose a bending-resistant and compression-insensitive
flexible circuit consisting of a bottom thick Cu layer and an LM healing layer (Figure 1(a-iii)). When cracks
propagate in the Cu film during bending, LM can fill and bridge the cracks in real-time through spontaneous
interfacial wetting, thus enhancing the bending stability of the flexible circuits. Meanwhile, the rigid thick Cu
layer can withstand higher pressure under compression, which enables the resistance of the circuit being less
affected by squeezing, thereby achieving a win-win combination of excellent bending durability and
compression insensitivity. A comparison of the scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of the Cu circuit

whereas that of the Cu-LM circuit increased by only 0.11%, demonstrating that the thick Cu layer plays an

30, 53-59], as it can withstand more bending cycles under extremely small bending radii (<1 mm) while
maintaining very low resistance changes. Such excellent bending durability and conductivity are attributed to
the real-time healing of cracks by the highly fluidic LM, as well as the inherently excellent electrical
conductivity and ability to maintain the shape of solid Cu film under extremely small bending radii, which
avoids possible flow interruption of pure LM due to squeezing of the channel under extremely small bending

solution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and bulk LM. Here, the Cu pattern was obtained by photolithography
and wet etching (Figures S2 and S3). The Cu/PI film we used is the commercially available flexible copper
clad laminate (FCCL), i.e., PI‒Cu laminate, which is used for manufacturing flexible PCBs in the industry.
This Cu/PI film exhibits excellent adhesion between Cu and PI. We tested the adhesion between Cu and PI by
the Scotch tape peeling test [60] and pull‑off test [61]. As shown in Movie S1, the etched Cu pattern remains
intact after the Scotch tape peeling test. Moreover, in the pull‑off test (Figure S4 and Movie S2), the Cu layer
did not detach from the PI substrate even under a maximum pulling force of 14.429 MPa. No residual Cu was
observed on the dolly, and the failure occurred preferentially at the interface between the PI and the underlying
steel block. Such strong adhesion between Cu and PI is beneficial for the bending performance of the flexible
circuit. The sticky surface oxides of LM often adhere to various surfaces without selectivity, making it
difficult to manipulate and pattern LM [62]. Considering that oxides can react with acid or alkaline solutions
[63, 64], we dripped LM into a solution of NaOH. Due to the higher density of LM, it sank beneath the NaOH
solution, forming a distinctly two-layer solution. Fortunately, during this natural stratification process, the
surface oxides of LM were removed by the NaOH solution. In this way, by a simple and efficient dip-coating
method, the non-oxidized LM can selectively adhere onto the surface of the Cu pattern without leaving residue
on the PI surface (Figure 2(a-i)). The significant difference in adhesion between Cu and PI surfaces is due to
the distinct wettability of the non-oxidized LM on these two surfaces. As shown in Figure 2(a-ii), the LM
droplet treated with NaOH (aq) exhibits non-wetting behavior on the PI surface with a contact angle of 127°,
whereas it can wet well on the Cu film with a contact angle of 25°. This wettability difference enables the
selective adhesion of the LM to the Cu surface, as seen from the comparison of optical images before and after
dip-coating in Figure 2(a-iii). LM completely covered the Cu surface with clear edges, while there was no
residue on the PI substrate. Therefore, the selective wetting behavior of LM on the Cu pattern facilitates the
printing of LM, allowing it to serve as a downstream process compatible with traditional high-resolution and
high-efficiency photolithography and etching processes.
The uniformity of LM adhering to the Cu surface is critical to the consistent electrical properties of flexible
circuits. We observed that the spontaneously wetted LM on the Cu surface formed a relatively regular arc
shape, which remained stable due to the formation of surface oxides upon exposure to air. Therefore, the
height of the LM exhibits an approximate geometric relationship determined by the line width and contact
angle, as shown in Figure 2(b). To verify this relationship, a series of lines with different widths (Figure 2(c))
were printed, and the heights of the LM were measured by laser confocal microscope. The experimental
results are generally in agreement with the theoretical curve, indicating the correctness of the geometric
relationship (Figure 2(d)). This self-wetting-dependent geometric relationship provides a foundation for the
uniform amount of LM printed on the Cu surface and enhances the controllability of printing. The
applicability of this method for printing patterns across a wide span of line widths was further demonstrated by

The capability to fabricate large-area complex patterns with various line widths is of great significance
for the efficient manufacturing of complex flexible circuits. Meanwhile, whether LM and Cu can coexist
stably over the long term is also an issue that needs to be explored, as it relates to whether they can maintain
their respective liquid and solid states to fulfill their complementary roles in enhancing bending stability and
compression insensitivity. As a demonstration, we fabricated a large-area complex pattern of traditional
Chinese gardens through a simple dip-coating process. As shown in Figure 3(a), LM fully covered all parts
of the Cu patterns with different line widths, demonstrating the feasibility and high efficiency of this method
for printing large-area complex patterns. To investigate whether LM and Cu can coexist stably over a long
period of time, we analyzed the morphology and interfacial element composition of the flexible circuit
stored for 60 days in an ambient environment. As shown in Figure 3(a-iii), the LM and Cu visually retained
their respective original colors. Furthermore, the element compositions of three different locations of the
cross-section of the Cu-LM flexible circuit were analyzed by field emission scanning electron microscope
(SEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). Figure 3(b-i) shows the element composition of the top
layer. Three elements, gallium (Ga), indium (In), and tin (Sn), were present in this layer, which corresponded
exactly to the three components of the LM. At the interface between Cu and LM, both Cu and Ga were
present, confirming the occurrence of an alloying reaction between LM and Cu [65]. However, in the bottom
layer, only Cu was observed, indicating that the alloying reaction did not penetrate further downward. The
element composition at the above three locations indicates that the alloying reaction occurred only at the
interface between the LM and Cu after long-term storage, while the top layer and the bottom layer still
maintained their original bulk LM and Cu, respectively. This indicates that the two layers of LM and Cu in
the flexible circuit can coexist for a long time. This is attributed to the fact that the reaction between LM and
Cu stops after their reaction product (CuGa2) reaches a certain thickness, as CuGa2 acts as a barrier to
further reaction [50, 66-69]. The thickness of the CuGa2 layer is typically 3–5 μm at room temperature [50,
69]. Consequently, conventional nanoscale metal layers may be fully dissolved by LM, which mainly acts as
a wetting layer for printing LM. In contrast, our thick Cu layer (13 μm) retains a portion of the unreacted Cu
at the bottom, which can continue to provide electrical conductivity. It is worth noting that the Cu-Ga
compounds formed at the interface can effectively drive the wetting of LM on the Cu surface [50]. Therefore,
this interfacial alloying reaction is actually beneficial, as it can enhance the wettability and adhesion
between LM and Cu, which is helpful for the real-time healing of cracks generated on the Cu film and
improving the bending durability of the flexible circuit.

(Figure S7), demonstrating that the flexible circuit can remain stable over a long time. This stable resistance

Benefiting from the real-time healing of cracks, compared with that of the conventional Cu circuit, the
bending durability of the Cu-LM flexible circuit is significantly improved. To investigate the bending
durability of the circuits, we tested the cyclic bending performance of these two types of flexible circuits at a
bending radius of 0.5 mm (Figure 4(a)) and a bending frequency of 5 Hz. The initial resistance of the Cu
circuit is approximately 2 Ω, and that of the Cu-LM circuit is approximately 1.4 Ω. As shown in Figure 4(b),
during the bending process, the resistance changes of both circuits generally went through three stages,
namely, the stable stage, the stage of dramatic increase in resistance, and the stage of failure. For the Cu
circuit, the resistance began to increase rapidly after approximately 99 000 cycles, with a maximum
resistance change of 912% (Figure 4(b-i)). In contrast, the stable stage of the Cu-LM circuit can persist up to
approximately 230 000 cycles, with a maximum resistance change of only 130% (Figure 4(b-ii)). By
comparing the resistance changes of these two circuits during the bending fatigue tests (Figure 4(c)), we find
that the bending durability of the Cu-LM circuit is significantly better than that of its counterpart Cu circuit.
This improvement in bending resistance is attributed to the real-time healing of fatigue cracks by LM. As
shown in Figure 4(d), by observing the unencapsulated circuits subjected to the same bending cycles as the

at the Cu circuit after cyclic bending (Figure 4(d-i)). Such cracks will open up under bending and further

To elucidate the healing mechanism of the circuit, we observed the dynamic filling process of LM at the
cracks in the Cu film under an optical microscope. Here, a thicker Cu film (300 m) was applied for
observation because it can generate more noticeable cracks under fewer bending cycles, thus facilitating the
capture of the dynamic cracking and filling process in a shorter time. As shown in Movie S3 and Figure 4(e),
as the number of bending cycles increased, cracks gradually initiated and expanded in the Cu film.
Meanwhile, LM spontaneously filled them in real-time. Moreover, LM deformed conformally during the
dynamic opening and closing of the crack, and no voids were observed at the interface between LM and the
crack, indicating the good wettability of LM at the Cu crack interface. Therefore, LM can fill the Cu cracks
and heal the conductive pathways, thereby extending the bending lifespan of the circuit. The increase in
resistance before complete fracture, as shown in Figure 4(b-ii), may be attributed to the electrical
conductivity of LM being lower than that of Cu. Therefore, after the crack is filled with LM, the resistance
slightly increases compared with that of the original continuous and intact Cu layer. We further analyzed the
possible reasons for the ultimate failure of the circuit (Figure S8). As the number of bending cycles further
increases, the cracks in the Cu layer further propagate and grow in size, and slight interface delamination
may occur in the Cu layer near the crack due to the high stress around the crack (as shown in Figure 1(b)).
This can cause the Cu crack to open significantly during bending so that LM is unable to fully fill such a
large crack gap in the bending state, leading to a large change in resistance and ultimate failure of the circuit.
We further investigated the effect of the bending frequency on the stability of the circuit. As shown in
Figure 4(f)–(h), with increasing bending frequency, the bending durability of the circuit decreases.
Specifically, at a bending frequency of 20 Hz, the resistance increased by 396% after 193 000 cycles. When
the frequency was increased to 40 Hz, the relative resistance change reached 550% after 164 000 cycles. We
attribute the decrease in the durability of the circuit with increasing bending frequency to two possible
reasons. On the one hand, a higher bending frequency may influence immediate repair due to the
viscoelasticity and inertial effects of LM. On the other hand, an increased bending frequency may accelerate
the propagation of cracks in the Cu film, thereby reducing the bending durability of the circuit.

The real-time healing of cracks ensures improved operational stability and extended lifespan for the
flexible circuit, making it particularly suitable for ensuring the stability of long-term continuous signal
monitoring of wearable systems that inevitably undergo deformations. It is worth noting that the practical
applications of Cu-LM flexible circuits require not only their own stability but also stable interconnections
with other electronic components. To this end, we first investigated the connection stability between flexible
circuits and electronic components. As a qualitatively intuitive demonstration, the flexible circuit was
interconnected with 16 LEDs and standard connectors, forming a flexible 4×4 LED array (Figure 6(a)). This
LED array can maintain stable lighting under bending, which preliminarily proves that the flexible circuit
can stably connect with other electronic devices. To further quantitatively investigate the connection
reliability, we observed the interface status between a resistor (50 Ω) and the flexible circuit and measured
the current‒voltage (I‒V) characteristics under different bending angles. As shown in Figure 6(b), the
electrodes at both ends of the resistor can be spontaneously wetted by LM after treatment with HCl vapor
[49], as evidenced by the meniscus formed by the wetting of the LM. This demonstrated that flexible circuit
could form a good electrical connection with the resistor. This method for stably interconnecting electronic
components via LM is also commonly used in other literature [79-81]. The wetting effect occurs because
LM undergoes interfacial alloying reactions with the metal coating on the pins of the electronic components.
As reported in a previous study [49], for the interface between the Ga-based LM and the pins of rigid
electronic components, the possible reactions are mainly the alloying reaction between Ga and gold (Au) or
palladium (Pd), while the nickel (Ni) coating can serve as a barrier layer to prevent LM from further reacting
with the underlying Cu layer of the pins. Subsequently, the circuit was encapsulated with PDMS, which is
intended to ensure the mechanical stability of the electrical connection. To validate the reliability of the
interfacial connections, we measured the I‒V characteristics under 10°, 60°, 150° bending, and 180° torsion
conditions. The resulting four I‒V curves overlap well with each other, demonstrating that the flexible circuit
can maintain stable interfacial connections with negligible contact resistance variation under varying
deformation states.

3. Conclusion
We have shown an extremely bending-resistant and compression-insensitive flexible circuit achieved by
the real-time healing of fatigue cracks in the bottom Cu layer via the spontaneous interfacial wetting of the
upper LM. Moreover, the thick bottom Cu layer plays an important role in maintaining conductivity under
compression to enhance the compression insensitivity of the circuit. The etched Cu pattern template in the
bottom layer also facilitates the printing of LM by selective interfacial wetting, allowing LM to leverage the
manufacturing advantages of Cu pattern inherited from conventional photolithography and etching,
achieving high-resolution and high-efficiency printing. The obtained flexible circuit can maintain its original
stable bilayer morphology over a long time, with alloying reactions occurring only at the interface without
further downward penetration. Profiting from the real-time healing of fatigue cracks, compared with the
counterpart Cu circuits, the bending-resistant flexible circuit achieved excellent durability of 230 000 cycles
under a bending radius of 0.5 mm and 60 000 cycles under repeated folding cycles, achieving improvements
of 2.3 and 120 times, respectively, whereas its resistance fluctuation under compression is only 0.05% of
that of the counterpart LM circuit. As a demonstration, a flexible signal acquisition system constructed with
this circuit can continuously capture pulse signals during bending and remain functional after 10 000
bending cycles. The simultaneously enhanced bending stability and compression insensitivity greatly boost
the applicability and reliability of flexible circuits under various deformation conditions.
4. Experimental section
4.1 Materials
Liquid metal (galinstan) with the melting point of 6–9 °C was purchased from Yunnan Zhongxuan Liquid
Metal Technology Co., Ltd. Polyimide-copper laminate (PI is 25 µm thick and copper film is 13 µm thick)
was purchased from Shenzhen Bangkai Adhesive Products Co., Ltd. PDMS (SYLGARD 184) curing agent
and elastomer were purchased from Dow Corning. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), ferric chloride (FeCl3), and
hydrochloric acid (HCl) were purchased from Aladdin.
4.2 Wet etching Cu patterns
The Cu patterns on PI film were prepared by conventional photolithography and wet etching. The
detailed process is as follows. As shown in Figure S3, the commercially available Cu/PI film was cut into
the required dimensions and attached to a rigid PET film via electrostatic adsorption to facilitate the

subsequent lithography process. A layer of photoresist (EPG535) was spin-coated on the PI-Cu film (500
rpm for 15 s and then 1 500 rpm for 40 s), followed by baking on a hot plate at 90 °C for 7 min. Then, the
sample was exposed to the UV light of a lithography machine for 8 s under the cover of a photomask with
customized patterns. Subsequently, it was developed in 0.5 wt% NaOH solution for 12 s. Then, the sample
with the photoresist pattern was wet-etched for 40 s at 50 °C in a mixed solution of FeCl3 (40 wt%) and HCl
(37 wt%) with a volume ratio of 3:1, followed by removing the photoresist using acetone and ethanol to
obtain the Cu pattern (Figures S2 and S3).
4.3 Fabrication of the Cu-LM flexible circuits
LM was adhered to the Cu patterns by a simple dip-coating method in naturally stratified NaOH (aq) (30
wt%, top layer) and bulk LM (bottom layer). Firstly, LM was dripped into the NaOH solution. During this
process, the surface oxides of LM were removed by the NaOH solution, ultimately forming a stratified
solution with NaOH solution on the top layer and non-oxidized LM at the bottom layer. Next, dip-coating
process was conducted by immersing the Cu pattern into the LM. LM can selectively wet and uniformly coat
onto the Cu surface with no residue on the PI surface. Then the flexible circuit was obtained by
encapsulating with PDMS (prepolymer and curing agent at a mass ratio of 10:1).
4.4 Characterization and measurements
SEM images were obtained by a field-emission scanning electron microscope (SU8010, HITACHI). The
microscopic optical images of the Cu pattern, Cu-LM pattern, and height of LM were obtained by a laser
scanning confocal microscope (OLS4000, Olympus). The contact angles were recorded by a contact angle
goniometer (Dataphysics, OCA20). To test the long-term bending durability of the Cu-LM circuits and Cu
circuits, a customized stretching machine consisting of a stepping motor, a stepping motor controller, a
sliding block, a screw, and guide rails was used to perform bending cycles. The bending angle was regulated
by controlling the displacements. The cyclic folding tests were conducted by a shaker (SINOCERA JZK-10),
which was driven by an excitation signal from the function generator (Agilent 33220A) amplified by a
power amplifier (SINOCERA YE5871A). The compression tests were conducted by a uniaxial testing
machine (PT1198GTD, POOTAB). The resistance changes and current‒voltage (I‒V) characteristics during
the bending process were monitored by a source meter (B2912A, Keysight).
